swozey · Nov 28, 2026

It's just an administrator/orchestrator for containers. If you start a docker container without kubernetes (docker/podman run) there's nothing to "orchestrate" it, as in if it crashes the kubernetes server restarts it, moves it to less loaded nodes, ties it to its storage, etc. You can even have it manage vms and other stuff.

This is assuming you know what a container is of course but you don't need to know cgroups or syscalls in depth to understand that k8s just keeps them running and moving around how you want.

It's a giant go api server in the end, "is nginx still running 3 containers? only one? start two more."

xg15 · Nov 28, 2026

Yes, but much in the same sense that websites could already run JavaScript code before. I.e., that part isn't new, and it runs in the same sandbox, so there is no security breach.

What's new is that it runs an entire Linux kernel on it and also emulates the structure of a Kubernetes cluster - so the cluster can assign your tab workloads, route requests to it, etc.

As with all those demos where "the server sends requests to the page" instead of the usual other way around, it's probably implemented using a WebSocket or WebRTC connection to the demo's server. The page has to open that connection first, but once it's open, both page and server can exchange arbitrary messages, so that's often used to make server-driven pages.

But this means your machine is not open to receive arbitrary packets, it all has to go through that one connection.

It all doesn't really do much except contributing some bit of compute resources from your machine to their cluster while you have the tab open - and giving you a log view so you can watch it receiving requests and feel proud.
